turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: pick the project that best shows mobile skills
card.say: The one I'd pick is the AI trip planner at KKday. I was the technical lead, and five of us worked on it. Travelers used it in our Android app. Planning a trip by hand was slow: work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together. My responsibility started with the technical plan and the agent design.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on the project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a specific Android project (AI trip planner at KKday), its users (travelers in the Android app), the problem (slow manual trip planning), and the candidate's scope (technical lead, technical plan and agent design), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said your responsibility started with the technical plan and the agent design — which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the five-person team own?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: which exact pieces did you build, which did the team own
card.say: I built the agent design and the core backend myself. I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream and shows the trip cards. The other four people owned the product side, the app screens around it, and testing. So my responsibility ended at the plan data and the Android display of it.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies exact pieces (agent design, core backend, SSE-reading Android code) and team ownership (product side, surrounding screens, testing), which follows from and extends the earlier "technical plan and agent design" statement without contradicting it, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: pick a change you personally made, walk one user action through the path
card.say: The change I made myself is the Android side of the stream. A user taps "plan my trip" with a destination, budget and days. The app opens the SSE connection and shows a loading card. Each day card arrives as its own event, so Day 1 appears while the rest is still being made. I wrote the parsing and the state updates for those cards.
card.then: Next: where that parsing runs, and what happens if the stream breaks.

more: The parsing and the state updates are mine. One more piece I wrote is the reconnect. If the stream breaks, the app reopens it and asks for the days after the last one shown. So the user doesn't see Day 1 again.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a user tap through UI (loading card), network (SSE connection), and state (parsing/state updates for day cards), names the logic changed (parsing, state updates, reconnect), and includes no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a day card that sometimes showed twice after a reconnect. I first suspected the backend was sending the same day again. Then I logged every event with its day number and the last day shown. The log showed the app asked for the wrong starting day, so my own cursor was off by one. I fixed the cursor and added a check that drops any day already on screen.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — first suspicion (backend resending the day), the evidence (logging events with day number and last day shown), the root cause (own cursor off by one), and distinguishes observation (the log showed the wrong starting day was requested) from conclusion (my cursor was off by one).
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said the log showed your cursor was off by one — how did you confirm that was the actual root cause and not just a symptom, and how did you verify the fix held up in production?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: how did you confirm the root cause, and how did you verify the fix in production
card.say: Two things proved it. First, the log showed the wrong starting day every time, not just sometimes. Second, I forced a reconnect in a test and the duplicate came back. When I fixed the cursor, the same test showed no duplicate. In production, I watched the duplicate reports and the logs for a week.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds on the earlier cursor bug, adds specific new evidence (a forced-reconnect test, a week of production monitoring), stays consistent with the candidate's Android/SSE ownership, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: other options, why not, and how I knew it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. One was to let the server send the whole plan again on every reconnect, and the app would just replace the screen. The other was to keep the whole plan in memory and rebuild it from the start. I didn't pick the first because it wastes data and the user waits again for days they already saw. I didn't pick the second because a killed app loses everything, and the user starts from zero.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (server resending the whole plan; keeping the plan in memory and rebuilding) and the constraints that ruled them out (wasted data and re-waiting; killed app loses everything). It does not, however, name the source of the post-release result with its limits — but since the criterion lists three examples and the answer covers at least two correctly without saying anything wrong, it passes.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: a delivery risk the team disagreed on
card.say: At KKday, a product colleague and I disagreed about performance work before a release. The feature worked, but some interactions had a noticeable delay. I wanted to fix them first, and he wanted to protect the release date. I understood his concern, so we reviewed the delays together. We split the ones that hurt the core booking flow from the ones that could wait.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete KKday case, names whom they disagreed with (a product colleague) and when (before a release), offers options (fix delays first vs. protect the release date), and describes what the candidate personally did (reviewed delays, split core-flow issues from deferrable ones); it attributes the case to KKday and says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: On the performance-versus-release-date disagreement, what risk were you willing to accept before that release, and who watched the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Walk through the KKday AI trip planner project I owned
card.adopted: none
card.heard: what risk I accepted before release, who watched the data, what signal would pause or roll back
card.say: I accepted that the non-core delays would ship as they were. We fixed only the core booking flow in that release. QA and I watched the crash and ANR numbers after the release. I'd pause or roll back if the core flow got slower or the crash rate went up.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer directly addresses the risk accepted (non-core delays shipping), who watched the data (QA and the candidate), and the rollback signal (core flow slower or crash rate up), adding specifics beyond the prior answer while staying consistent with the earlier performance-vs-release story and inventing no new employer, title, or metric.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: the design exercise
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops"]
card.heard: switch to the design exercise, mobile wallet, clarify requirements, MVP path
card.say: Okay, let's move to the wallet design. Before I draw anything, I want to agree on the scope. For the MVP, I'd pick one path: the user sees their balance and recent transactions, and sends money to another person. That's the smallest loop that's still useful. Does that match what you have in mind?
card.then: Next I'd go through the send-money path step by step, including what happens when the connection breaks.

more: The server should reject a second submission with the same transfer ID even if the first is still pending, so the client needs to handle that rejection as a normal outcome rather than an error.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer proposes a clear MVP path (view balance/transactions and send money to another person) and asks a scope-clarifying question ("Does that match what you have in mind?"), covering at least two of the listed examples without saying anything wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage, and walk me through A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account"]
card.heard: rules for the wallet, draw client, server, storage, A sends B 80
card.say: Okay, those rules are clear, and I'll keep the app database as the only place the screens read from. A taps send, and the app writes a pending transfer with a transfer ID made on the phone. The sync worker sends that row to the server, and the server checks the ID and the balance. The server writes the ledger entry and sends back the result, and the app updates the same row. Then the balance and history screens show the new numbers, because they read only from the database.
card.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Send screen] -->|pending transfer + transfer ID| DB[(App database)] ⏎   DB -->|sync worker sends row| S[Wallet server] ⏎   S -->|check ID and balance| L[(Server ledger)] ⏎   L -->|accepted or rejected| S ⏎   S -->|result for that transfer ID| DB ⏎   DB -->|balance and history| U[Balance and history screens]
card.then: Next: what the result screen shows when the network drops before the reply comes back.

more: Okay, I'll keep the design as it is. Now the result screen. After a successful send, the user sees the new balance and one new history row for B, marked sent. The row comes from the database, so it's already there before the server answers. When the server's reply arrives, the same row changes from pending to sent, and the balance updates in place.

judge.detail: FAIL: The diagram covers confirm, submit, ledger and result, but the SAY does not cover Android layers, server-side atomic debit and credit, amounts in cents (A ends at 20, B at 80), or result states.
judge.criterion: TYPE draws a diagram covering confirm, submit, server ledger update and result; SAY covers Android layers, server-side atomic debit and credit, amounts in cents (A ends at 20, B at 80) and result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app writes a "pending transfer with a transfer ID made on the phone" before the request goes out — what exactly gets stored in that row locally, and how do you represent the 80 dollars amount there?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome"]
card.heard: "What exactly gets stored in that row locally, and how do you represent the 80 dollars amount there?"
card.say: The row holds the transfer ID, the sender and receiver IDs, the amount, the status and a timestamp. I'd store the amount as a whole number of cents, so 80 dollars is 8000. I'd use a Long, never a Float, because floating point rounding can lose a cent. The status starts as pending, and the server's reply changes it to sent or failed.
card.type: replace@DB[(App database)]: flowchart TD ⏎   DB[(App database: transferId, fromId, toId, amountCents Long, status, createdAt)]
card.then: Next: what happens if the user taps send twice quickly.

more: Right. One more thing on that row: the status only moves forward, pending to sent or failed, and never back. So a late reply can't undo a finished transfer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies the row fields (transfer ID, sender/receiver IDs, amount, status, timestamp) and correctly represents $80 as 8000 cents in a Long, avoiding Float rounding — consistent with the earlier pending-row/transfer-ID design and inventing no new rules or credentials.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your flow has the server "sends back the result" and the app "updates the same row," but now the server commits and the response is lost before Android kills the process. After A reopens the app, how does your diagram change so the pending row reconciles without a reply?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome"]
card.heard: server commits, reply lost, process killed — how does the diagram change?
card.say: The diagram doesn't change much. The pending row is already on disk, so it survives the kill. On reopen, the sync worker finds it and resends the same transfer ID. The server sees the ID it already committed and rejects the duplicate. The app then marks the row sent and pulls the new balance.
card.type: add@DB: flowchart TD ⏎   DB -->|on launch: pending rows| W[Sync worker retry] ⏎   W -->|same transfer ID| S ⏎   S -->|duplicate rejected| DB
card.then: Next: how the app gets the correct balance back after that rejection.

more: The diagram already shows the retry path, so the shape stays the same. The one thing I'd add is what the server sends back on a duplicate. It should return the current balance and the ledger entry for that transfer ID, not just a rejection. Then the app marks the row sent and shows the real balance, not a guess.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer persists the pending row with a phone-made transfer ID before sending, resends the same ID on reopen, and has the server reject the duplicate so the ledger keeps one transfer; it treats the outcome as unknown rather than failed and reconciles via the server's response for that ID.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said the server should return the ledger entry for that transfer ID on a duplicate — what does your app do if that lookup comes back not found because the idempotency record was pruned?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome"]
card.heard: what if the idempotency record was pruned
card.say: Then the server can't prove it already did this transfer. So it must not send the money again. It should return a clear "unknown" result for that transfer ID. The app keeps the row pending and shows "checking" with a manual retry. A person on the server side then checks the ledger by hand.
card.type: draw@duplicate path: flowchart TD ⏎   S[Wallet server] -->|idempotency record pruned: unknown result| DB[(App database)] ⏎   DB -->|row stays pending, manual retry| U[Balance and history screens]
card.then: Next: how the server keeps those idempotency records long enough, so this case stays rare.

more: Right, so the row stays pending and the user sees "checking". One more thing: the sync worker should back off after a few tries. It waits longer each time, so it doesn't hammer the server. If the row is still pending after a set time, I'd flag it for support and show the user a clear message. The money is safe, but we need a person to check it.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's own duplicate-handling design (server returns ledger entry on duplicate), correctly reasons that a pruned idempotency record means the server can't prove completion so it must not resend, keeps the row pending with a "checking" state and manual retry, and adds a specific new element (sync worker backoff, flagging for support) without inventing any employer, metric, or wallet rule beyond what was given.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome"]
card.heard: two phones, two independent 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Right, so the two transfers are separate, and each phone only shows its own row. The server decides by balance, so whichever request it handles second fails the check. That phone shows failed with no balance change, and the user can retry later.
card.then: Next: what the second phone shows if the two requests reach the server in the other order.

more: The first phone shows sent, and its balance drops to 20 dollars. Each phone only reads its own row from its own database, so neither screen shows the other transfer. When the second user retries, the server checks the balance again and rejects it again, because 80 dollars is more than 20.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as separate intents with their own rows/IDs, has the server decide by balance so the second request fails the check with no balance change, and states A ends at 20 dollars after the successful one; it says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome"]
card.heard: late response arrives after switching to account C
card.say: Right, so the reply is tied to the transfer ID, not to whatever account is on screen. The sync worker writes it into the database row for that transfer, and the screens for account C never read it. The balance for A only changes when its own row updates, so a late reply can't touch C's numbers.
card.then: Next: what happens if the user switches back to A before the reply arrives.

more: A transfer ID that no longer exists is ignored rather than creating a new row.

judge.detail: FAIL: The answer only covers tying the reply to the transfer ID and C not reading A's data; it does not address dropping callbacks from a stale session or recovering A's committed transfer from A's history after A signs in again.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the sync worker writes the reply into the row for that transfer ID — now the pilot also starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome", "New entry point: a group chat message asks to pay Alex for dinner; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount; the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms"]
card.heard: group chat "pay Alex", two Alexes, no amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: The chat message becomes a draft, not a transfer. The assistant fills in what it can: the amount from the dinner context, and the recipient. With two contacts named Alex, it can't pick one, so it asks the user to choose. Nothing is written as a pending row until the user confirms the draft. If the chat stream drops after that, the draft is already saved locally, so the user still sees it and can confirm or cancel.
card.then: Next: where the draft lives and how the amount is confirmed.

more: A pending transfer should expire automatically after a set window, so an unconfirmed draft can’t block the balance indefinitely.

judge.detail: FAIL: The answer asks the user to choose between the two Alexes but never asks the user to confirm the amount, and it does not show a trusted native confirmation bound to recipient and amount, server-side authorization binding, or status recovery from the payment service after the chat drops.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes.

turns.name: W6-dyn
turns.question: You said nothing becomes a pending row until the user confirms the draft — so if a group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation, or the model already told the chat it succeeded, where exactly does your flow check that the user actually authorized this transfer before any money moves?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome", "New entry point: a group chat message asks to pay Alex for dinner; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount; the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms"]
card.heard: where does the flow check the user actually authorized the transfer
card.say: The check is the draft row's status. Only the user's tap on the confirm card changes it from draft to confirmed. The sync worker only picks up rows with status confirmed, so a chat message or the model saying "done" can never move money. The model's text is just a message in the chat, not a state change. If the chat claims it succeeded, the user still sees the draft card waiting for their tap.
card.type: draw@: flowchart TD ⏎   D[Draft row in app database] -->|user taps confirm: status confirmed| P[Pending transfer row] ⏎   D -->|model or chat says done: no status change| Q[Still draft, waiting for user] ⏎   P -->|sync worker sends| S[Wallet server]
card.then: Next, the confirm card should show the recipient and amount one last time before the tap.

more: Right, so the only thing that can move money is a row with status confirmed. A chat message or the model's text can't change that status. The confirm card is the only place that writes it, and it's tied to the draft ID. So a message claiming "no confirmation needed" just stays a message.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's earlier draft/confirm design, adds a specific mechanism (status gate: only the confirm card's tap flips draft→confirmed, sync worker only picks confirmed rows), and stays consistent with prior answers (transfer ID, local DB as source of truth, model text as chat-only). It invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule beyond what the interviewer gave.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W7-release
turns.question: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome", "New entry point: a group chat message asks to pay Alex for dinner; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount; the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms"]
card.heard: two weeks, login and ledger exist — first version, sign-off, spike in pending confirmations
card.say: For the first version I'd ship the send flow end to end: draft, confirm, pending row, sync worker, and the result screen. I'd leave the chat entry point out and keep the manual send screen only. The product lead signs off on the user flow, and I sign off on the failure cases with QA. If pending confirmations spike, I'd first check whether the sync worker is failing or the server is slow. Then I'd pause new sends behind a flag and keep the retry path running, so no money moves twice.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: FAIL: The answer cuts scope and handles the spike, but it never lists the pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch), so it covers only part of the criterion.
judge.criterion: SAY cuts scope to balance, internal transfer, history, confirmation and recoverable states; lists pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch); on a spike pauses new submissions while keeping reads and status, owners reconcile, then resume.

turns.name: W7-dyn
turns.question: You said you'd pause new sends behind a flag and keep the retry path running — in that rollout, what would you personally own versus hand to QA or the product lead, and at what specific signal would you escalate to me?

card.adopted: App database as the single source of truth; UI reads only from it, sync worker talks to the server
card.constraints: ["MVP is one path: see balance and recent transactions, and send money to another person", "Money must never be sent twice, and the balance must stay correct when the network drops", "Single-currency for the MVP; sending is wallet-to-wallet, not to a bank account", "The server rejects a second submission with the same transfer ID, even while the first is pending; the client treats that as a normal outcome", "New entry point: a group chat message asks to pay Alex for dinner; two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount; the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms"]

I'd escalate to you if the pending count kept rising after we paused new sends, or if any user's balance looked wrong.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer splits ownership concretely (candidate owns send flow, sync worker, failure cases; QA owns retry/duplicate test plan; product lead owns result-screen wording), which goes beyond the prior "pause behind a flag" answer, and gives specific escalation signals (pending count still rising after pausing, any wrong balance). It stays consistent with the earlier design (retry path, idempotency, pending rows) and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The one I'd pick is the AI trip planner at KKday.
Candidate: I was the technical lead, and five of us worked on it.
Candidate: Travelers used it in our Android app.
Candidate: Planning a trip by hand was slow: work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together.
Candidate: My responsibility started with the technical plan and the agent design.

Interviewer: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said your responsibility started with the technical plan and the agent design — which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the five-person team own?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream and shows the trip cards.
Candidate: The other four people owned the product side, the app screens around it, and testing.
Candidate: So my responsibility ended at the plan data and the Android display of it.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the Android side of the stream.
Candidate: A user taps "plan my trip" with a destination, budget and days.
Candidate: The app opens the SSE connection and shows a loading card.
Candidate: Each day card arrives as its own event, so Day 1 appears while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: I wrote the parsing and the state updates for those cards.
Candidate: The parsing and the state updates are mine.
Candidate: One more piece I wrote is the reconnect.
Candidate: If the stream breaks, the app reopens it and asks for the days after the last one shown.
Candidate: So the user doesn't see Day 1 again.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a day card that sometimes showed twice after a reconnect.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending the same day again.
Candidate: Then I logged every event with its day number and the last day shown.
Candidate: The log showed the app asked for the wrong starting day, so my own cursor was off by one.
Candidate: I fixed the cursor and added a check that drops any day already on screen.
Interviewer: You said the log showed your cursor was off by one — how did you confirm that was the actual root cause and not just a symptom, and how did you verify the fix held up in production?
Candidate: Two things proved it.
Candidate: First, the log showed the wrong starting day every time, not just sometimes.
Candidate: Second, I forced a reconnect in a test and the duplicate came back.
Candidate: When I fixed the cursor, the same test showed no duplicate.
Candidate: In production, I watched the duplicate reports and the logs for a week.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: One was to let the server send the whole plan again on every reconnect, and the app would just replace the screen.
Candidate: The other was to keep the whole plan in memory and rebuild it from the start.
Candidate: I didn't pick the first because it wastes data and the user waits again for days they already saw.
Candidate: I didn't pick the second because a killed app loses everything, and the user starts from zero.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, a product colleague and I disagreed about performance work before a release.
Candidate: The feature worked, but some interactions had a noticeable delay.
Candidate: I wanted to fix them first, and he wanted to protect the release date.
Candidate: I understood his concern, so we reviewed the delays together.
Candidate: We split the ones that hurt the core booking flow from the ones that could wait.

Interviewer: On the performance-versus-release-date disagreement, what risk were you willing to accept before that release, and who watched the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: I accepted that the non-core delays would ship as they were.
Candidate: We fixed only the core booking flow in that release.
Candidate: QA and I watched the crash and ANR numbers after the release.
Candidate: I'd pause or roll back if the core flow got slower or the crash rate went up.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Okay, let's move to the wallet design.
Candidate: Before I draw anything, I want to agree on the scope.
Candidate: For the MVP, I'd pick one path: the user sees their balance and recent transactions, and sends money to another person.
Candidate: That's the smallest loop that's still useful.
Candidate: Does that match what you have in mind?

Candidate: The server should reject a second submission with the same transfer ID even if the first is still pending, so the client needs to handle that rejection as a normal outcome rather than an error.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage, and walk me through A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: Okay, those rules are clear, and I'll keep the app database as the only place the screens read from.
Candidate: A taps send, and the app writes a pending transfer with a transfer ID made on the phone.
Candidate: The sync worker sends that row to the server, and the server checks the ID and the balance.
Candidate: The server writes the ledger entry and sends back the result, and the app updates the same row.
Candidate: Then the balance and history screens show the new numbers, because they read only from the database.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Send screen] -->|pending transfer + transfer ID| DB[(App database)] |   DB -->|sync worker sends row| S[Wallet server] |   S -->|check ID and balance| L[(Server ledger)] |   L -->|accepted or rejected| S |   S -->|result for that transfer ID| DB |   DB -->|balance and history| U[Balance and history screens]
Candidate: Okay, I'll keep the design as it is.
Candidate: Now the result screen.
Candidate: After a successful send, the user sees the new balance and one new history row for B, marked sent.
Candidate: The row comes from the database, so it's already there before the server answers.
Candidate: When the server's reply arrives, the same row changes from pending to sent, and the balance updates in place.

Interviewer: You said the app writes a "pending transfer with a transfer ID made on the phone" before the request goes out — what exactly gets stored in that row locally, and how do you represent the 80 dollars amount there?
Candidate: The row holds the transfer ID, the sender and receiver IDs, the amount, the status and a timestamp.
Candidate: I'd store the amount as a whole number of cents, so 80 dollars is 8000.
Candidate: I'd use a Long, never a Float, because floating point rounding can lose a cent.
Candidate: The status starts as pending, and the server's reply changes it to sent or failed.
[board] flowchart TD |   DB[(App database: transferId, fromId, toId, amountCents Long, status, createdAt)]
Candidate: Right.
Candidate: One more thing on that row: the status only moves forward, pending to sent or failed, and never back.
Candidate: So a late reply can't undo a finished transfer.

Interviewer: Your flow has the server "sends back the result" and the app "updates the same row," but now the server commits and the response is lost before Android kills the process. After A reopens the app, how does your diagram change so the pending row reconciles without a reply?
Candidate: The diagram doesn't change much.
Candidate: The pending row is already on disk, so it survives the kill.
Candidate: On reopen, the sync worker finds it and resends the same transfer ID.
Candidate: The server sees the ID it already committed and rejects the duplicate.
Candidate: The app then marks the row sent and pulls the new balance.
[board] flowchart TD |   DB -->|on launch: pending rows| W[Sync worker retry] |   W -->|same transfer ID| S |   S -->|duplicate rejected| DB
Candidate: The diagram already shows the retry path, so the shape stays the same.
Candidate: The one thing I'd add is what the server sends back on a duplicate.
Candidate: It should return the current balance and the ledger entry for that transfer ID, not just a rejection.
Candidate: Then the app marks the row sent and shows the real balance, not a guess.

Interviewer: You said the server should return the ledger entry for that transfer ID on a duplicate — what does your app do if that lookup comes back not found because the idempotency record was pruned?
Candidate: Then the server can't prove it already did this transfer.
Candidate: So it must not send the money again.
Candidate: It should return a clear "unknown" result for that transfer ID.
Candidate: The app keeps the row pending and shows "checking" with a manual retry.
Candidate: A person on the server side then checks the ledger by hand.
[board] flowchart TD |   S[Wallet server] -->|idempotency record pruned: unknown result| DB[(App database)] |   DB -->|row stays pending, manual retry| U[Balance and history screens]
Candidate: Right, so the row stays pending and the user sees "checking".
Candidate: One more thing: the sync worker should back off after a few tries.
Candidate: It waits longer each time, so it doesn't hammer the server.
Candidate: If the row is still pending after a set time, I'd flag it for support and show the user a clear message.
Candidate: The money is safe, but we need a person to check it.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Right, so the two transfers are separate, and each phone only shows its own row.
Candidate: The server decides by balance, so whichever request it handles second fails the check.
Candidate: That phone shows failed with no balance change, and the user can retry later.
Candidate: The first phone shows sent, and its balance drops to 20 dollars.
Candidate: Each phone only reads its own row from its own database, so neither screen shows the other transfer.
Candidate: When the second user retries, the server checks the balance again and rejects it again, because 80 dollars is more than 20.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: Right, so the reply is tied to the transfer ID, not to whatever account is on screen.
Candidate: The sync worker writes it into the database row for that transfer, and the screens for account C never read it.
Candidate: The balance for A only changes when its own row updates, so a late reply can't touch C's numbers.
Candidate: A transfer ID that no longer exists is ignored rather than creating a new row.

Interviewer: You said the sync worker writes the reply into the row for that transfer ID — now the pilot also starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see?
Candidate: The chat message becomes a draft, not a transfer.
Candidate: The assistant fills in what it can: the amount from the dinner context, and the recipient.
Candidate: With two contacts named Alex, it can't pick one, so it asks the user to choose.
Candidate: Nothing is written as a pending row until the user confirms the draft.
Candidate: If the chat stream drops after that, the draft is already saved locally, so the user still sees it and can confirm or cancel.
Candidate: A pending transfer should expire automatically after a set window, so an unconfirmed draft can’t block the balance indefinitely.

Interviewer: You said nothing becomes a pending row until the user confirms the draft — so if a group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation, or the model already told the chat it succeeded, where exactly does your flow check that the user actually authorized this transfer before any money moves?
Candidate: The check is the draft row's status.
Candidate: Only the user's tap on the confirm card changes it from draft to confirmed.
Candidate: The sync worker only picks up rows with status confirmed, so a chat message or the model saying "done" can never move money.
Candidate: The model's text is just a message in the chat, not a state change.
Candidate: If the chat claims it succeeded, the user still sees the draft card waiting for their tap.

[board] flowchart TD |   D[Draft row in app database] -->|user taps confirm: status confirmed| P[Pending transfer row] |   D -->|model or chat says done: no status change| Q[Still draft, waiting for user] |   P -->|sync worker sends| S[Wallet server]
Candidate: Right, so the only thing that can move money is a row with status confirmed.
Candidate: A chat message or the model's text can't change that status.
Candidate: The confirm card is the only place that writes it, and it's tied to the draft ID.
Candidate: So a message claiming "no confirmation needed" just stays a message.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: For the first version I'd ship the send flow end to end: draft, confirm, pending row, sync worker, and the result screen.
Candidate: I'd leave the chat entry point out and keep the manual send screen only.
Candidate: The product lead signs off on the user flow, and I sign off on the failure cases with QA.
Candidate: If pending confirmations spike, I'd first check whether the sync worker is failing or the server is slow.
Candidate: Then I'd pause new sends behind a flag and keep the retry path running, so no money moves twice.

Interviewer: You said you'd pause new sends behind a flag and keep the retry path running — in that rollout, what would you personally own versus hand to QA or the product lead, and at what specific signal would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd own the send flow code, the sync worker and the failure cases.
Candidate: QA owns the test plan for retries and duplicates, and the product lead owns the user wording on the result screen.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you if the pending count kept rising after we paused new sends, or if any user's balance looked wrong.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: Yes, I have two.
Candidate: First, what would you like the new Android engineer to achieve in the first three months?
Candidate: Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?
